en.intro: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how inner discipline takes shape in daily life. He has just finished bodily austerity and now moves to how we use our voice.
en.notice: Krishna names the austerity of speech. It is about words that do not agitate the listener, that are true, pleasant, and beneficial.
en.next: After speech, Krishna turns to the austerity of the mind, where silence and self-control take over.
en.meaning: Speech that does not agitate, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with study and practice, is called austerity of speech.

en.intro: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how inner discipline takes shape in daily life. He has just finished bodily austerity and now moves to how we use our voice.
en.body: Speech that does not agitate, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with study and practice, is called austerity of speech. Krishna names the austerity of speech. It is about words that do not agitate the listener, that are true, pleasant, and beneficial. After speech, Krishna turns to the austerity of the mind, where silence and self-control take over.

hi.body: जो वाक्य उद्वेग न करनेवाला, सत्य, प्रिय और हितकारक हो, तथा स्वाध्याय और अभ्यास हो, उसे वाङ्मय तप कहते हैं। वाणी के बाद, कृष्ण मन के तप की बात करते हैं, जहाँ मौन और आत्म-संयम होता है।

issues: en.notice: banned phrase "not just about what you say, but"

meaning_changed: "उसे वाङ्मय तप कहते हैं" (The source uses 'वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते' (is called austerity of speech). The Hindi translation changes the grammatical structure to 'उसे वाङ्मय तप कहते हैं' (one calls it austerity of speech), which shifts the meaning from a formal designation to a general statement and alters the exact phrasing.)

unsupported: "सुनने वाले को अशांत न करें" (The source says 'अनुद्वेगकरं' (not causing agitation). The Hindi notice adds the unsupported detail 'सुनने वाले को' (to the listener) and 'अशांत' (agitated), which is not in the source.)

borrowed: "Notice: यह सिर्फ यह नहीं कि आप क्या बोलते हैं, बल्कि यह है कि आपके शब्द सुनने वाले को अशांत न करें" (This is a direct borrowing from the NEXT verse (17.16), which describes mental austerity (serenity of mind) and the need for words not to disturb the listener. It is incorrectly attributed to the austerity of speech in this verse.)
